newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks to see limited upside.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks to see limited upside.

text.p: Japanese stocks are likely to see a limited upside this coming week, with the market remaining wary of an uncertain economic outlook for the start of a new financial year in April.
Market participants were also waiting to see if there would be any government measures to boost real estate liquidity, which would help help prop up Japan's sluggish economy.
But hopes for the land policies could be overshadowed by hangovers from a series of corporate scandals revealed this month.
On Friday, the Nikkei 225 average finished at 17,923.64, down 275.1 points from its closing on March 7.
"We are anxious to see if the market can head up after the SQ," said Kenji Karikomi, a deputy general manager at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.

The settlement of the Nikkei 225's March futures and options, called "special quotations" (SQ), went relatively smoothly on Friday, removing downward pressure from the market, brokers said. Traders had expected small net selling related to the settlement.
Brokers said they would pay close attention to government policies to support the real estate market.
"Positive and negative aspects of the outlook for government policies have been mixed so far, but worries are slightly stronger now," said Akihiro Naemura, a strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
"Until some policies are unveiled, bank and construction shares cannot perk up," said a second-tier brokerage analyst.
Japanese banks and building firms have been saddled with huge bad loans, most of which are backed by land as collateral.
A National Land Agency source told Reuters earlier this month that the government was now thought unlikely to unveil in March a package of steps aimed at boosting land liquidity.
Market sentiment has been undermined by corporate scandals.
"Overall sentiment is not good, as there are worries about not only Nomura but Japanese securities houses in general," said Kazuo Shiogai, deputy branch manager at ING Baring Securities.
Shiogai also said the market was not confident about the state of the economy after the sales tax goes up by two percentage points to five percent in April.
Giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd said two of its directors had been involved in suspected illegal deals with a corporate client linked by Japanese media to a "sokaiya" racketeer.

On Friday, only hours after Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki and two board members resigned over the scandal, a police official told a parliamentary panel that the National Police Agency was gathering information on the affair.
Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said that the securities watchdog was likely to inspect other brokers with reported links with racketeers.
Ajinomoto Co Inc, Japan's top food processor, said earlier last week that two of its executives had been arrested on suspicion of paying company funds to racketeers.
The market is also likely to be weighed down by continuing profit-taking ahead of the end-March corporate book closings, brokers said.
